questions.stem: What is the first move when deducing the charge an atom will carry?

options.text: Count the electrons in the outer electron shell
options.explanation: The outer-shell count drives everything that follows; the method starts there.

options.text: Count all the electrons the atom holds
options.explanation: Total electrons describe the neutral atom; only the outer shell decides the charge.

options.text: Read the atomic number off the periodic table
options.explanation: Atomic numbers count protons; the charge comes from the outer electrons.

options.text: Memorise the charge with no method behind it
options.explanation: Memory helps, but the method backs it up when an unfamiliar ion appears.

questions.stem: An atom has fewer than four outer electrons. What does it do, and what follows?

options.text: It donates the electrons and becomes a positive ion
options.explanation: Fewer than four means giving is easier, and giving leaves a positive charge.

options.text: It receives electrons and becomes a negative ion
options.explanation: Receiving suits atoms already past four; this atom sits below the hinge.

options.text: It shares electrons to fill the shell
options.explanation: Sharing belongs to covalent bonding; charge deduction here assumes transfer.

options.text: It does nothing, being already stable
options.explanation: A shell short of a full set is not complete, so the atom reacts.

questions.stem: What charge does a group 2 metal ion carry?

options.explanation: Two outer electrons donated leaves the ion two units positive.
The negative sign belongs to receivers; group 2 metals donate.
That is group 1's charge; group 2 donates two electrons.
Three is the group 3 pattern; this row donates only two.

questions.stem: What charge does a group 6 non-metal ion carry?

options.explanation: Six outer electrons means two short of a full shell, so two arrive and the charge is 2-.
Non-metals receive rather than donate, so the sign stays negative.
The group number is not the charge; only the gap to a full shell counts.
That is group 7's pattern; group 6 needs two electrons.

questions.stem: What makes an ion a compound ion?

options.text: It is built from more than one element
options.explanation: Compound ions such as OH- and NH4+ carry several elements under one overall charge.

options.text: It carries a charge greater than 1
options.explanation: Charge size is unrelated; some single-element ions carry 2+ or 3-.

options.text: It forms only from transition metals
options.explanation: Compound ions are about joined elements, not about which block the metal sits in.

options.text: It is a molecule with no charge
options.explanation: Molecules are neutral; compound ions carry their charge like any other ion.

questions.stem: State what a compound ion is, and what its formula demands.
questions.modelAnswer: An ion made from more than one element — its formula must be learned as given.

questions.stem: State what kind of ion forms when an atom's outer electron count sits below four.
questions.modelAnswer: A positive ion — the atom donates its outer electrons.

questions.stem: Explain why a Group 7 atom ends up carrying a 1- charge.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a Group 7 atom has seven outer electrons — more than four — so it receives one electron to complete the shell, ending with one extra electron and a 1- charge.

questions.stem: A neutral atom has the configuration 2,8,3. State whether it donates or receives electrons, and the charge of the ion it forms.
questions.modelAnswer: It has 3 outer electrons — fewer than four — so it donates all three and forms a 3+ ion.

questions.stem: Which formula and charge belong to the silver ion?

options.explanation: Silver sits outside the group rules with its own fixed charge of 1+.
A 2+ pattern from nearby metals does not transfer to silver.
No table row gives silver a 3+; its charge is fixed at 1+.
Silver is a metal, and metals appear on the positive side only.

questions.stem: Iron appears in the table twice. Which pair of charges does it carry?

options.explanation: Iron(II) is Fe2+ and iron(III) is Fe3+; both rows are assumed knowledge.
No row shows iron at 1+; the pair is 2+ with 3+.
Dropping the iron(III) row loses half the pair.
Negative signs belong to the non-metal and compound-ion side.

questions.stem: What is the formula and charge of the zinc ion?

options.explanation: The table lists Zinc(II) at 2+, one fixed charge.
Zinc does not follow the group 1 pattern; it is a named metal at 2+.
That is the group 3 pattern, not zinc's.
Zinc sits on the positive side; the negative sign cannot apply.

questions.stem: Which is the correct formula and charge for the nitrate ion?

options.explanation: Nitrate is the compound ion: one nitrogen with three oxygens, charge 1-.
That is the group 5 single-element pattern; nitrate is the compound ion, not a lone nitrogen.
That is the carbonate ion's label; nitrate carries one oxygen fewer and a single negative charge.
Nitrate is a negative ion; the table lists it at 1-.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches compound ion to formula and charge?

options.explanation: Both rows come straight from the tables: ammonium positive at 1+, carbonate negative at 2-.
Both signs are backwards: ammonium is the positive one, carbonate the negative.
The ammonium subscript is 4, and carbonate's charge is 2-, not 1-.
Ammonium carries a single positive charge, and carbonate carries 2-, so both halves are wrong here.

questions.stem: Name the five compound ions the table says to know, with their charges.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydroxide OH-, ammonium NH4+, carbonate CO3 2-, nitrate NO3- and sulfate SO4 2-.

questions.stem: State the ion that hydrogen rides as in the common-ions table.
Explain why iron appears twice in the common-ions table.
questions.modelAnswer: Because iron forms two different positive ions — Fe2+ and Fe3+ — depending on how many electrons it loses.

questions.stem: A compound contains potassium ions and carbonate ions. State each ion's charge and the overall formula of the compound.
questions.modelAnswer: Potassium (Group 1) gives K+; carbonate is CO3 2-; two K+ ions balance one carbonate, so the formula is K2CO3.
